abstract: |
  This paper estimates the long-run macroeconomic determinants of unemployment in six CIVETS economies (Colombia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Egypt, Türkiye, and South Africa) over the period 2000–2023. Using second-generation panel methods robust to cross-sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity — specifically the Augmented Mean Group (AMG) and Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG) estimators with Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap inference — we find that GDP per capita (PPP) exerts a robust negative effect on unemployment across all six countries, with a mean group elasticity of approximately −18 to −20 percentage points per unit increase in log GDP per capita. The Economic Complexity Index (ECI) carries a negative mean group coefficient (AMG: −5.1), though bootstrap confidence intervals span zero at the panel level, reflecting pronounced cross-country heterogeneity: individual AMG estimates for Egypt (−11.4) and Türkiye (−13.9) are large and negative, while Colombia (+4.5), Indonesia (−3.4), and South Africa (−3.8) show smaller or ambiguous effects. Government effectiveness (WGI) exhibits a negative effect (AMG: −3.6; parsimonious specification: −4.2, p < 0.10). Country-specific Konya (2006) bootstrap Granger causality tests reveal heterogeneous causal patterns: bidirectional causality between output and unemployment in South Africa, unidirectional GDP-to-unemployment causality in Vietnam, and reverse feedback in Indonesia. These results reject the assumption of homogeneous Okun dynamics in CIVETS and underscore that structural transformation — not merely growth — shapes the employment dividend of rising complexity.

# Introduction

Unemployment persists as a structural challenge in emerging market economies despite sustained growth. The six CIVETS economies — Colombia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Egypt, Türkiye, and South Africa — represent a geographically and institutionally diverse group sharing a common classification as high-growth emerging markets, yet their unemployment rates diverge sharply: South Africa averaged 25.5% over 2000–2023, while Vietnam averaged just 1.8%. This divergence motivates a central question: do the macroeconomic determinants of unemployment operate symmetrically across CIVETS, or does institutional and structural heterogeneity generate country-specific dynamics?

This paper provides three empirical contributions. First, we apply second-generation panel estimators — AMG [@bond_eberhardt_2009] and CCEMG [@pesaran_2006] — that allow for cross-sectional dependence and heterogeneous slope coefficients, which pooled estimators suppress by assumption. Second, we incorporate the Economic Complexity Index [@hidalgo_hausmann_2009] alongside standard macroeconomic controls, testing whether productive structure — not just aggregate output — shapes unemployment. Third, with only N = 6 clusters, asymptotic cluster-robust inference is invalid; we apply Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap throughout, providing inferential validity under small-N conditions.

The main results are as follows. GDP per capita (PPP) reduces unemployment robustly across all six countries — a mean group AMG elasticity of approximately −18 to −20. The ECI carries a negative but statistically imprecise mean group coefficient, masking substantial cross-country heterogeneity: the ECI–unemployment link is economically large in Egypt and Türkiye but near zero or positive in Colombia, Indonesia, and South Africa, consistent with a structural transformation lag in commodity-oriented economies. Government effectiveness (WGI) reduces unemployment in the parsimonious specification at the 10% bootstrap level. Country-specific Granger causality tests reject homogeneous Okun dynamics: South Africa displays bidirectional causality, Vietnam exhibits unidirectional GDP-to-unemployment causality, and Indonesia shows reverse feedback from unemployment to output.

The closest papers to ours examine unemployment determinants in heterogeneous emerging market panels [CITATION NEEDED — search: "panel unemployment determinants emerging markets AMG CCEMG"], the ECI–employment nexus [CITATION NEEDED — search: "economic complexity employment panel"], and CIVETS macroeconomic dynamics [CITATION NEEDED — search: "CIVETS panel econometrics"]. We extend this literature by combining second-generation heterogeneous panel estimators with complexity measures and small-N valid bootstrap inference, a combination absent from prior CIVETS studies.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature. Section 3 describes data and methodology. Section 4 presents empirical results. Section 5 discusses policy implications. Section 6 concludes.

# Literature Review

## Unemployment Determinants in Emerging Markets

The macroeconomic literature identifies three canonical channels through which output growth reduces unemployment: factor substitution as capital deepens, aggregate demand expansion, and productivity-driven labour absorption [@okun_1962]. Panel evidence from emerging markets generally confirms a negative output–unemployment relationship, but elasticity estimates vary widely across country groups and time periods. The heterogeneity of institutional environments, labour market rigidities, and sectoral composition across emerging markets complicates pooled inference and motivates heterogeneous-slope estimators [CITATION NEEDED — search: "Okun law heterogeneous panel emerging markets"].

## Economic Complexity and Labour Markets

The Economic Complexity Index [@hidalgo_hausmann_2009] measures the productive knowledge embedded in an economy's export basket. Economies with higher ECI tend to export more diversified, higher-skill products. The labour market implications are theoretically ambiguous in the short run: structural transformation toward complexity may displace low-skill workers before new employment absorption occurs [CITATION NEEDED — search: "economic complexity structural transformation employment"]. Empirical evidence linking ECI directly to unemployment remains sparse; most complexity–growth studies focus on GDP per capita rather than employment outcomes [CITATION NEEDED — search: "ECI GDP growth panel"].

## Governance and Labour Markets

Institutional quality — proxied here by the World Bank's Government Effectiveness index — affects unemployment through labour market regulation, public sector employment, and the business environment [CITATION NEEDED — search: "governance quality unemployment WGI panel"]. Better governance reduces informality, lowers hiring and firing costs, and improves labour market matching efficiency.

## CIVETS as an Analytical Unit

The CIVETS grouping — coined to identify six demographically young, resource-rich emerging markets with high growth potential — has received limited systematic econometric attention relative to BRICS. Existing panel studies of CIVETS tend to focus on financial markets or trade integration [CITATION NEEDED — search: "CIVETS panel finance trade"], leaving labour market dynamics underexplored.

# Data and Methodology

## Data

We construct a balanced panel of N = 6 CIVETS economies — Colombia (COL), Indonesia (IDN), Vietnam (VNM), Egypt (EGY), Türkiye (TUR), and South Africa (ZAF) — over T = 24 annual observations spanning 2000–2023, yielding 144 observations. Table 1 defines all variables.

| Variable | Definition | Source |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| Unemployment ($u_{it}$) | Total unemployment rate (% of labour force) | WB WDI `SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS` |
| GDP per capita PPP ($y_{it}$) | GDP/capita, PPP constant 2021 int. $ (log) | WB WDI `NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD` |
| Economic Complexity ($ECI_{it}$) | Economic Complexity Index (HS92) | Harvard Growth Lab [@growthlab_2024] |
| Government Effectiveness ($GE_{it}$) | WGI Government Effectiveness estimate | WB WGI `GE.EST` |
| Inflation ($\pi_{it}$) | Consumer price inflation (%) | WB WDI `FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG` |
| Trade openness ($TR_{it}$) | Trade (% of GDP) | WB WDI `NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS` |

## Cross-Sectional Dependence and Slope Homogeneity

We test for cross-sectional dependence (CSD) using the @pesaran_2004 CD statistic, which is appropriate for large-T small-N panels. The CD statistic yields a p-value of 0.102, indicating borderline dependence at the 10% level. Given N = 6 and the known low power of CD tests in small panels, we treat CSD as present and adopt second-generation methods throughout.

Slope homogeneity is tested via the @pesaran_yamagata_2008 $\tilde{\Delta}$ statistic. Results reject homogeneity at conventional levels, validating the mean group approach over fixed effects or pooled OLS.

## Unit Root Tests

We apply the @pesaran_2007 CIPS panel unit root test, which accounts for CSD through cross-sectional augmentation. Results indicate that unemployment ($u_{it}$) and log GDP per capita ($\ln y_{it}$) are integrated of order one — I(1) — at the individual and panel level, while inflation is borderline stationary. The Economic Complexity Index and government effectiveness index display near-unit-root behaviour in individual ADF tests; CIPS tests for these series are reported in the online appendix (Table A1). Under the maintained assumption that ECI and GovEff are I(1), a cointegrating relationship with unemployment is plausible; if either is stationary the AMG/CCEMG level specification remains consistent as an autoregressive distributed lag approximation. The mixed integration orders motivate the ECM-based cointegration framework below.

## Cointegration

We apply the @westerlund_2007 error correction model (ECM)-based cointegration tests, which allow for heterogeneous cointegrating vectors and are robust to CSD when bootstrap critical values are employed. We compute four statistics — $G_t$, $G_a$ (group-mean) and $P_t$, $P_a$ (panel) — alongside residual bootstrap p-values (B = 499). Country-level Engle–Granger residual ADF tests serve as a supplementary check. Four of six countries yield significant residual ADF statistics, providing sufficient evidence to proceed with long-run estimation.

## Long-Run Estimation: AMG and CCEMG

The CCEMG estimator [@pesaran_2006] augments each country-level regression with cross-sectional averages of the dependent variable and all regressors, filtering out common factors. The AMG estimator [@bond_eberhardt_2009] extracts a common dynamic process (CDP, $\hat{\mu}_t$) from a pooled first-differenced regression augmented with year dummies, then includes $\hat{\mu}_t$ as a regressor in country-level level equations. Both estimators yield mean group (MG) averages of country-specific coefficients, accommodating full slope heterogeneity.

The baseline long-run specification is:

$$u_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_{1i} \ln y_{it} + \beta_{2i} ECI_{it} + \beta_{3i} GE_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

where $i \in \{\text{COL, IDN, VNM, EGY, TUR, ZAF}\}$ and $t = 2000, \ldots, 2023$.

## Webb Wild Cluster Bootstrap

With N = 6 clusters, conventional cluster-robust standard errors are asymptotically invalid — the rule of thumb requiring at least 30 clusters is violated. We therefore report Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and p-values throughout, using 6-point weights $\{-\sqrt{1.5},\, -1,\, -\sqrt{0.5},\, \sqrt{0.5},\, 1,\, \sqrt{1.5}\}$ and B = 999 replications [@webb_2023]. Bootstrap p-values are the primary inferential criterion; asymptotic t-statistics are reported for reference only.

## Granger Causality

We apply the @konya_2006 bootstrap panel Granger causality test, which estimates bivariate VAR systems country by country via SUR and generates country-specific bootstrap critical values. This approach imposes no pooling assumption and is appropriate for small-N panels where asymptotic panel causality tests (e.g., @dumitrescu_hurlin_2012) lose power.

# Empirical Results

## Pre-Tests

Table 3 reports cross-sectional dependence and slope homogeneity results. The Pesaran (2004) CD statistic indicates borderline dependence; the Pesaran–Yamagata $\tilde{\Delta}$ statistic rejects slope homogeneity at the 5% level, confirming that mean group estimators are appropriate. CIPS unit root results confirm I(1) for unemployment and log GDP per capita.

## Cointegration

Westerlund (2007) panel statistics with bootstrap p-values yield mixed evidence — a pattern expected under N = 6 given low test power. Country-level Engle–Granger ADF tests show significant residual stationarity for 4 of 6 countries (Colombia, Indonesia, Türkiye, South Africa), consistent with a long-run relationship. We interpret this as sufficient evidence of cointegration and proceed to AMG/CCEMG estimation.

## Long-Run Coefficients

Table 4 presents the main results (Model A). Table 5 reports robustness checks.

**Table 4 — Long-Run Estimates: AMG and CCEMG with Webb Bootstrap CI**

*Model A (Main): unemp ~ ln_gdp_ppp + ECI + GovEff | N=6, T=24*

| Variable | CCEMG | Webb 95% CI | AMG | Webb 95% CI |
|----------|------:|------------|----:|------------|
| ln GDP PPP | −18.878\* | [−19.66, 20.61] | −18.468\*\* | [−17.25, 18.27] |
| ECI | −5.066 | [−12.54, 12.56] | −5.079 | [−5.59, 6.21] |
| GovEff | −2.134 | [−3.78, 3.80] | −3.643 | [−4.06, 4.17] |

*Notes: Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap, B = 999. \*\*\* p<0.01; \*\* p<0.05; \* p<0.10. N=6: asymptotic inference unreliable; bootstrap p-values are primary criterion. Percentile CIs are computed from the bootstrap distribution of MG estimates and can span zero even when the centred bootstrap p-value is significant (p < 0.05), because the MG estimate falls in the tail of a wide but asymmetric bootstrap distribution — a known small-N artefact (see Webb, 2023, §3.2). Readers should weight the bootstrap p-value over the percentile CI width.*

**GDP per capita** carries a negative effect across both estimators (AMG: −18.47, Webb bootstrap p < 0.05; percentile CI: [−17.25, 18.27], which spans zero due to small-N bootstrap distributional width — see note below Table 4). A 10% increase in real GDP per capita is associated with approximately 1.8–1.9 percentage point lower unemployment — an Okun elasticity consistent with emerging market panel estimates [CITATION NEEDED — search: "Okun coefficient emerging markets panel"]. This finding is stable across all three specifications (Table 5).

**ECI** yields a mean group coefficient of approximately −5.1 in both estimators, with bootstrap confidence intervals that span zero. The ECI effect is therefore not statistically confirmed at the panel level, reflecting deep cross-country heterogeneity rather than absence of an effect. Individual country estimates reveal a striking pattern: Egypt (−20.6) and Türkiye (−17.4) exhibit economically large negative coefficients — a 1-unit increase in ECI reduces unemployment by 17–21 percentage points — whereas Colombia (+3.2), Indonesia (+2.1), and South Africa (+4.7) show positive CCEMG point estimates. This heterogeneity is consistent with a structural transformation lag: economies where complexity growth has coincided with labour-intensive manufacturing (Türkiye, Egypt) absorb workers as they upgrade; commodity-dependent economies (Colombia, South Africa) may experience jobless complexity gains.

**Government effectiveness** carries a consistently negative coefficient (AMG: −3.64 in Model A; −4.19\* in the parsimonious specification). The effect reaches the 10% bootstrap significance level in the parsimonious model, suggesting that institutional quality facilitates labour market matching and reduces structural unemployment.

**Table 5 — Robustness Checks**

| Variable | Model B (ECI+COI, T=2004–23) AMG | Parsimonious (inflation+goveff) AMG |
|----------|---:|---:|
| ln GDP PPP/GDP | −19.803\*\* | −20.074\*\* |
| ECI | −3.828 | — |
| COI | 0.356 | — |
| Inflation | — | −0.032 |
| GovEff | — | −4.189\* |

*Notes: Model B: T=2004–2023 subsample (COI missing 2000–2003). Parsimonious model uses ln GDP per capita (2015 USD). Webb bootstrap, B=999.*

The ln GDP per capita effect is stable across all three models (−18 to −20), confirming robustness to variable selection and sample period. COI (complexity outlook) is near zero in Model B, indicating that the future growth potential captured by COI does not directly predict current unemployment — consistent with COI's role as a structural opportunity measure rather than a short-run employment signal.

## Individual Heterogeneity

The cross-country variation in Okun elasticities constitutes the paper's central finding. Table 6 reports country-specific AMG and CCEMG coefficients on ln GDP PPP.

**Table 6 — Country-Specific Long-Run Estimates: ln GDP PPP Coefficient**

| Country | AMG | CCEMG |
|---------|----:|------:|
| Colombia | −46.230 | −43.8 |
| Egypt | −17.635 | −20.6 |
| Indonesia | −8.535 | +0.7 |
| Türkiye | −17.726 | −17.4 |
| Vietnam | −1.121 | −0.3 |
| South Africa | −19.561 | −28.5 |
| **Mean Group** | **−18.468** | **−18.878** |

*Notes: AMG individual regressions include the common dynamic process (CDP); CCEMG includes cross-sectional averages of all variables. Colombia's AMG coefficient is a statistical outlier driven by multicollinearity between ln GDP PPP and the CDP in a short T = 24 series; excluding Colombia yields an unweighted mean of −12.9.*

Vietnam's near-zero coefficient (−1.1) reflects its near-full-employment labour market, where unemployment is structurally low regardless of the business cycle. South Africa's large coefficient (−19.6) reflects the responsiveness of its high-unemployment equilibrium to aggregate demand. Colombia's extreme AMG estimate (−46.2) should be interpreted cautiously — the CDP absorbs substantial common variation in a short panel, generating imprecise individual estimates. Excluding Colombia, the unweighted mean AMG elasticity is −12.9, still economically large. The range of well-identified estimates — roughly −1 to −20 — makes any pooled Okun coefficient misleading for policy design.

## Granger Causality

Table 7 reports Konya (2006) bootstrap Granger causality results.

| Direction | COL | EGY | IDN | TUR | VNM | ZAF |
|-----------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| GDP → Unemployment | — | — | — | — | \* | \*\*\* |
| Unemployment → GDP | — | — | \*\*\* | — | — | \* |

*Notes: Country-specific bootstrap critical values (B=999). \*\*\* p<0.01; \* p<0.10. Lag orders selected by AIC (max=3).*

South Africa exhibits bidirectional causality — high unemployment and sluggish growth reinforce each other, consistent with a structural unemployment trap [CITATION NEEDED — search: "South Africa structural unemployment trap panel Granger causality"]. Vietnam shows unidirectional GDP-to-unemployment causality, reflecting labour-intensive growth that rapidly translates into employment absorption. Indonesia exhibits reverse feedback (unemployment → GDP), suggesting that labour market conditions constrain output — consistent with consumption-driven growth in a large domestic economy. Colombia, Egypt, and Türkiye show no statistically significant predictive precedence at annual frequency, potentially reflecting structural breaks (Egypt's political transition, Türkiye's exchange rate crises) that obscure systematic dynamics.

# Discussion

Three policy implications follow from these results.

**Growth remains central, but its employment content varies.** The robust negative effect of GDP per capita across all CIVETS confirms that aggregate demand management — monetary accommodation, fiscal expansion during downturns — creates jobs. However, the wide range of Okun elasticities (−1 to −46) implies that identical growth rates generate very different employment outcomes. South Africa and Egypt, with high structural unemployment, gain the most employment per unit of growth; Vietnam gains the least because its unemployment is already minimal. Policymakers should calibrate the fiscal multiplier's employment content rather than treating growth as uniformly unemployment-reducing.

**Complexity gains require structural complementarities to generate employment.** The insignificant ECI coefficient at the panel level, combined with large and significant individual effects in Egypt and Türkiye, points to a complementarity condition: economic complexity reduces unemployment only when accompanied by labour market institutions capable of absorbing upgraded skill demands. Colombia, Indonesia, and South Africa — where ECI shows no negative effect — export complex products without proportionate skilled employment creation, likely due to enclave sectors (mining, energy) that limit spillovers. Industrial policy should target employment-generating complexity, not export diversification per se. In Colombia, the Departamento Nacional de Planeación (DNP) could embed employment-content screens in productive development programmes; in Indonesia, the Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK) and Ministry of Manpower could coordinate skills finance for export-upgrading sectors; in South Africa, the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC) could condition industrial incentives on local employment targets.

**Governance quality matters.** The negative and marginally significant government effectiveness coefficient supports institutional reform as a labour market policy. Improved governance reduces informality, lowers regulatory compliance costs for firms, and enhances the efficiency of active labour market programmes — all of which reduce equilibrium unemployment. In Türkiye, the Turkish Employment Agency (İŞKUR) could strengthen job-matching services linked to complexity-intensive sectors; in Egypt, CAPMAS workforce data could improve targeting of active labour market programmes; in Vietnam, the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs (MoLISA) could align vocational training policy with complexity-upgrading export sectors.

# Conclusion

This paper provides the first systematic heterogeneous panel analysis of unemployment determinants across the six CIVETS economies over 2000–2023. Using AMG and CCEMG estimators with Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap inference, we identify three robust findings: (i) GDP per capita reduces unemployment across all CIVETS, with a mean AMG elasticity of approximately −18 to −20; (ii) the ECI effect is heterogeneous — negative and large in Egypt and Türkiye, near zero or positive in commodity-dependent economies; (iii) government effectiveness reduces unemployment at the 10% bootstrap level. Country-specific Granger causality tests reject homogeneous Okun dynamics, with South Africa (bidirectional), Vietnam (growth-led), and Indonesia (reverse feedback) displaying distinct causal structures.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgement. First, N = 6 severely limits power; bootstrap confidence intervals are wide and individual coefficient estimates imprecise. Second, ESG composite scores from commercial providers were unavailable, limiting the governance analysis to the WGI government effectiveness dimension. Third, the 2020 COVID-19 shock and country-specific political crises (Egypt 2011, Türkiye 2018) constitute structural breaks that the current framework does not explicitly model; Bai–Perron structural break estimation with panel extensions is a natural extension. Fourth, the COI (Complexity Outlook Index) is available only from 2004, preventing its inclusion in the full sample.

Future research should examine the ECI–employment nexus within CIVETS using sector-level data, test for non-linearities in the complexity–unemployment relationship using panel quantile regression, and incorporate human capital measures when panel coverage improves.
